t: Why You Shouldn't Respond When A Difficult Student Has A Good Day student-has-a-good-day/
q: When a difficult student has a good day it’s normal to want to reward them for it.
But the truth is, the best response you can offer a difficult student after a good day is no response at all.
When you reward students for good behavior they become externally motivated.
Real and lasting change only happens when difficult students are intrinsically motivated to behave.
That isn’t to say that you should shun or ignore difficult students after a good day. You’ll just treat them like everyone else.
But how do you describe the view from the summit of Mount Everest?
x: Rewarding a difficult student's good day with prizes or effusive praise externalizes their motivation and cheapens the achievement.
Rewarding a difficult student's good day with prizes or effusive praise externalizes their motivation and cheapens the achievement.
Excessive celebration of good behavior can paradoxically signal the student is still viewed as an exception or outcast.
Good behavior should be treated as its own reward, since intrinsic motivation is necessary for lasting behavioral change.
Treating the student like everyone else after a good day, rather than singling them out, restores their sense of being a regular class member.
Linsin argues, counterintuitively, that the best response to a difficult student's good day is often no special response at all.

t: A Fun Way To Get Your Students To Follow Directions ections/
q: Following directions doesn’t improve by harping on it. It doesn’t improve by making a fuss about it or showing your frustration over it.
One such strategy is to slip a meaningless step into your directions. It’s a bit unorthodox, to be sure, but it’s remarkably effective.
A meaningless step, especially if it’s silly or out of the ordinary, causes students to listen more intently to your directions and better visualize what you want them to do.
One of the keys to improving following directions is to increase the challenge.
It isn’t a strategy you’ll want to use all the time, however. The novelty will wear off quickly if you put it into practice more than a couple times per week.
x: Following directions doesn't improve through frustration or repeated complaints—it improves through strategies that actively compel attention.
Linsin presents a strategy for improving how well students follow multi-step directions: inserting a deliberately meaningless, often silly step into an otherwise ordinary set of instructions.

t: A Gentle But Powerful Way To Increase Learning, Motivation, And Independence ning-motivation-and-independence/
q: So you teach this great lesson. Your students are really into it. They’re listening and participating.
You do for them what you know they can do for themselves. It’s exhausting, but you do it lesson after lesson and day after day

Their problem, you see, isn’t their inability. It’s not motivation, at least not directly. If they can pass your checks for understanding, then you’ve provided everything they need to work independently. The problem is learned helplessness.
Independence is a gift you give your students by gently withholding help for that which you know they can do themselves.
After finishing up a lesson, you’ll become a ghostly presence, neither ignoring nor helping, but just watching for signs of struggle
x: Students who freeze during independent practice often suffer from learned helplessness caused by excessive teacher support, not an inability to do the work.
Linsin diagnoses the problem of students who freeze up during independent practice not as an ability gap but as learned helplessness caused by excessive teacher hovering.

t: How To Give A Warning That Curbs Misbehavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/01/04/how-to-give-a-warning-that-curbs-misbehavior/
q: It’s a declaration of free grace you offer by letting them know that you are aware a rule has been broken.
Their warning is more of a threat than a courtesy. It’s the heavy hand of the law meted out with a glare and an air of intimidation.
Remember, you’re providing a service. What they do with the information is up to them.
A warning from you is like a red light that pops up on the dashboard of your car.
Done right, a warning is a statement of grace that acknowledges that we all make mistakes.

A properly delivered warning is a courtesy—an acknowledgment that a rule was broken, not a threat or display of anger.
